title: De Lyon à Tours: la reine qui convertit un royaume
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Le sang des Burgondes, the wound at the root (474-490)

stops.name: Lyon (Lugdunum), the Burgundian palace by the Saône
stops.campa: In the old Roman city of Lugdunum, where the Saône slides under the hill of Fourvière, a daughter is born to Chilperic, king of the Burgundians, and to his Catholic queen Caretena. They name her Chrotechildis: Clotilde. The Burgundian court is Arian, but the mother keeps the true faith burning in her rooms like a lamp carried through wind. The child is baptized Catholic in a heretic kingdom: the first fact of her life is already the shape of her whole war.
suggested_refs: Primatiale Saint-Jean, Lyon
Statue of Sainte Clotilde, Jardin du Luxembourg (Reines de France series)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.28, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Lyon, childhood among Arian kings
stops.campa: The girl grows in a court where four brother-kings divide one crown: Gundobad, Godegisel, Chilperic her father, Godomar. She learns Latin prayers at her mother's knee and Burgundian law in her father's hall. Bishops of the Catholic Gauls pass through and bless the little princess who is theirs in a palace that is not. Around her, under the feasting, the brothers watch one another the way wolves watch, and the child learns early that a kingdom is a thing that eats its own.
suggested_refs: Burgundian Lyon, quartier Saint-Jean

stops.name: Vienne, the family slaughter
stops.campa: The wolves close. Gundobad falls upon his brother's house: Chilperic is put to the sword, and the queen Caretena, the tradition gives her the river, is drowned, a stone bound at her neck, her body given to the Rhône. The two daughters are condemned to exile: Chrona, the elder, takes the veil of a nun; Clotilde, the younger, is kept where her uncle can see her. She is perhaps sixteen. Everything she will ever set in motion, the marriage, the conversion, the terrible Burgundian war of her sons, begins in this room.
stops.quote: Gundobad killed his brother Chilperic with the sword, and drowned his wife, tying a stone to her neck; her two daughters he condemned to exile: the elder, who became a nun, was called Chrona, the younger Clotilde.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.28
suggested_refs: Cathédrale Saint-Maurice de Vienne
The Rhône at Vienne
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.28, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: The Rhône below Vienne, the mother's grave
stops.campa: The river takes the queen and does not give her back. There is no tomb; the Rhône itself is the tomb, and every time Clotilde crosses running water for the rest of her life she crosses her mother. The canon is exact about the stone at the neck: the murderer wanted no floating witness. The orphan stands on the bank of the world with a dead father, a drowned mother, a sister bound for the cloister, and a soul that has just learned what it will spend seventy years answering.
suggested_refs: The Rhône in flood, Vienne reach
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.28, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Geneva, refuge with Chrona
stops.campa: The orphan girls are sent up the lake to Geneva, into the keeping of the murderer-uncle's watchmen. Chrona takes the veil; Clotilde lives beside her sister in something between a court and a convent. The tradition remembers her here as the servant of the poor: she washes the feet of pilgrims, carries bread to the beggars at the church door, keeps the hospice with her own hands. The city on the water becomes her novitiate. Gundobad thinks he has buried her in piety; God is aiming her.
suggested_refs: Cathédrale Saint-Pierre, Geneva
Chapel of the Maccabees

stops.name: Geneva, the beggar at the church door: Aurelian and the ring
stops.campa: A beggar in rags waits among the poor as Clotilde comes from Mass. She kneels to wash his feet as she washes all the others', and the beggar leans close. He is Aurelian, envoy of Clovis, king of the Franks, come disguised past Gundobad's spies. Into her palm, under the water, he presses the gold signet ring of his master. The princess does not startle. She hides the ring, hears the suit, and sends the beggar home with her answer sewn into his rags. The courtship of France is transacted in alms-water.
stops.quote: My master Clovis, king of the Franks, has sent me: he desires to take you for his wife.
stops.quote_source: Chronicle of Fredegar III.18 / Liber Historiae Francorum (the tradition)
suggested_refs: The ring of Clovis (the legend's sigillary ring)
19th-c. imagery of Aurelian kneeling before Clotilde

stops.name: Chalon-sur-Saône, the betrothal wrung from Gundobad
stops.campa: Clovis sends his embassy openly now, to Gundobad's own hall: he asks for Clotilde in marriage. The uncle who drowned her mother dares not refuse the king of the Franks: refusal is war, and he knows what the girl knows. Trembling between two fears, he chooses the nearer one and gives her up to the envoys. The wise Aridius is away in Constantinople; there is no counselor to whisper that this bride carries the memory of the Rhône with her. The betrothal is sealed; the carruca is made ready.
suggested_refs: Cathédrale Saint-Vincent, Chalon-sur-Saône

segments.name: La route de l'épousée, the bride's road (493)

stops.name: The Burgundian frontier near Langres, the carruca abandoned
stops.campa: The bridal wagon creaks north too slowly for a woman who knows her uncle's heart. Word flies behind her: Aridius has returned, and counsels Gundobad to snatch the bride back before she becomes a Frankish queen with a Frankish army. Clotilde orders the carruca abandoned, mounts a horse, and rides for the frontier at the gallop. At the edge of Burgundian land she bids her escort burn and pillage as they pass: the first fires of a vengeance she will feed for thirty years. Then she crosses, and is free.
stops.quote: I give thanks to Almighty God, for I see the beginning of the vengeance for my parents and my brothers.
stops.quote_source: Chronicle of Fredegar III / Liber Historiae Francorum (the tradition)
suggested_refs: The Langres plateau, old Roman road Lyon-Troyes

stops.name: Villery, near Troyes: the first meeting with Clovis
stops.campa: On the Roman road south of Troyes, at the place called Villariacum, the king of the Franks rides out to meet what his ring has won. Clovis has come down through Reims, Châlons, Arcis; Clotilde comes up from the burned frontier, and the tradition says she rode at the head of her own escort. The pagan king looks at the Catholic orphan of the Burgundians and is conquered before any bishop touches him. The two roads join and turn together toward Soissons. France, though nobody present can see it yet, begins at this crossroads.
suggested_refs: Village of Villery (Aube), the tradition's meeting place

stops.name: Soissons, the wedding of Clovis and Clotilde
stops.campa: In his capital of Soissons, in the hall where he once split the vase-breaker's skull, Clovis takes Clotilde to wife. The Frankish great men feast; the Burgundian bride, sixteen and orphaned by the man who signed her marriage contract, sits crowned beside a king who worships Wotan and the war-gods of his fathers. She has already begun the only campaign of her life: from the wedding night onward, the canon says, she never ceases urging her husband toward the God of her mother. The mission she will never drop is opened here.
suggested_refs: Abbaye Saint-Médard de Soissons
The vase of Soissons (the emblem of the reign)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.28, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

segments.name: La mission de la reine, the pagan king pressed toward her God (493-496)

stops.name: Soissons, the queen preaches to the king
stops.campa: In the royal chamber the queen wages her war of words. She tells the king his gods are carved things: Jupiter a defiler of his own kin, Mars and Mercury workers of sorceries, not lords of heaven. She sets against them the God who spoke the world, who hung the sun, who filled the sea. Clovis listens, shrugs, keeps his idols: all things were made at the nod of his gods, he answers. But the words lodge in him like arrowheads too deep to cut out. She does not stop. She never stops.
stops.quote: The gods you worship are nothing: they can help neither themselves nor others, for they are carved of stone or wood or metal.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29
suggested_refs: Grandes Chroniques de France illuminations of Clovis and Clotilde
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Soissons, Ingomer: baptized in white, dead in his robes
stops.campa: A first son is born, and the queen will not have him given to the idols: she has Ingomer baptized, the church hung with cloths, the font dressed like a bride. The child dies in the white robes of his baptism, within the week. The king's rage is a storm in the hall: had the boy been dedicated to his gods, he roars, he would surely have lived; baptized in the name of her God, he could not live at all. The queen stands in the ruin of her firstborn and answers with thanksgiving. Gregory carries the exchange word for word.
stops.quote: I give thanks to Almighty God, Creator of all things, who has not judged me unworthy, and deigns to take into His kingdom a child born of my womb.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29
suggested_refs: The white chrisom-robe (the baptismal dress of the Merovingian infants)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Soissons, Chlodomer sickens and is saved by her prayer
stops.campa: A second son, Chlodomer, and the unbroken queen carries him too to the font. The child sickens at once, and Clovis waits with grim arithmetic: baptized like his brother, he will die like his brother. The gods are keeping score. Clotilde goes to her knees and does not rise. She prays the fever down through the nights, and the child mends, and lives. The score the king was keeping turns in his hand: her God, prayed to, answers. It is the first miracle of her motherhood, worked on the son whose death at Vézeronce will one day break her.
suggested_refs: Font imagery of the Merovingian baptisms, Grandes Chroniques
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.29, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Tolbiac (Zülpich), the vow in the wreck of battle
stops.campa: Against the Alamanni at Tolbiac the Frankish line breaks and the slaughter turns on Clovis. His gods are silent in the din. Then the king lifts his eyes and his voice into the queen's heaven: Jesus Christ, whom Clotilde declares to be the Son of the living God, give me victory and I am yours. Even as the vow leaves him, the Alamanni waver; their king falls; the host that was devouring the Franks kneels to them. The battle is hers though she is a hundred leagues away: Tolbiac is won on her God's name, spoken with her name inside it.
stops.quote: Jesus Christ, whom Clotilde declares to be the Son of the living God... if Thou wilt grant me victory over these enemies, I will believe in Thee and be baptized in Thy name.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.30
suggested_refs: Ary Scheffer, 'Bataille de Tolbiac' (Versailles)
Zülpich, the Roman Tolbiacum
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.30, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Soissons, the king's secret and the summons to Remigius
stops.campa: The king comes home from the Alamannic war and tells the queen, secretly, how he won it: how he called on the name of Christ and the enemy melted. Clotilde wastes not an hour. She sends in secret to Remigius, bishop of Reims, bidding him come and bring to her husband the word of salvation while it is still warm in him. The bishop comes quietly to the court and begins to work the king's heart. Clovis hesitates once more: his people will not leave their gods, he says, and then his people, assembled, cry out with one voice that they will follow the deathless God.
suggested_refs: Saint Remigius (Remi), apostle of the Franks
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Reims, the city dressed for the font
stops.campa: Reims makes itself into a bride. The squares are shaded with painted cloths, the churches hung with white; candles burn in daylight and the baptistery breathes such perfumes, Gregory says, that the people think themselves set down among the odors of paradise. The queen moves through the preparations like the architect of an invisible cathedral finally seeing the vault closed: every hanging, every taper is a stone in the church she has been building since her wedding night. Tomorrow the kingdom kneels where she has prayed for three years.
suggested_refs: Basilique Saint-Remi, Reims
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Reims, the baptistery: the Sicamber bows, the dove descends
stops.campa: Christmas night. The new Constantine steps to the water, and Remigius speaks the sentence that France will keep forever: bow thy neck, Sicamber. Burn what thou hast adored, adore what thou hast burned. And when the press of the crowd blocks the clerk who bears the chrism, the bishop lifts his eyes and a dove whiter than snow comes down through the church bearing in its beak the ampulla of holy oil, the Sainte Ampoule that will anoint the kings of France to the end of kings. Clotilde stands beside the font. This is her victory; the water is her weapon.
stops.quote: Bow thy head meekly, O Sicamber; adore what thou hast burned, burn what thou hast adored.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31
suggested_refs: The Sainte Ampoule
Master of Saint Giles, 'The Baptism of Clovis' (National Gallery of Art, Washington)
Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Reims
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Reims, the three thousand and the king's sisters
stops.campa: Behind the king, the army: more than three thousand of his warriors go down into the water on the same night, the wolf-host of the Franks rising Christian from the font in their dripping thousands. The king's sister Albofled is baptized; his sister Lantechild, who had fallen into the Arian heresy of the Burgundian courts, confesses the Son equal to the Father and is anointed. One woman's stubbornness at one man's ear has just turned a people. Clotilde watches the army of her husband kneel to the God of her drowned mother.
stops.quote: Of his army, more than three thousand were baptized.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31
suggested_refs: The baptism of the 3000, Grandes Chroniques de France
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.31, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

segments.name: Les années de la reine: Paris (497-511)

stops.name: Paris: the queen in the new capital, Île de la Cité
stops.campa: After Vouillé and the breaking of the Visigoths, Clovis fixes his seat at Paris, in the old palace of the island where Julian was once raised on the shields. Clotilde is queen of a capital now. Four children live: Chlodomer whom her prayers pulled back from death, Childebert, Chlothar, and the girl Clotilde. In the city of Genevieve, the virgin who turned Attila with prayer as the queen turned a king, the two holy women of Paris pray in the same churches, and between them they are quietly deciding what France will be.
suggested_refs: Île de la Cité, site of the Merovingian palace
Sainte Geneviève, patroness of Paris
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.38, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Paris, the church of the Holy Apostles on Genevieve's hill
stops.campa: On the summit of the mons Lucotitius, above the left bank, king and queen raise a basilica to the apostles Peter and Paul, the church Clotilde has begged for, on the hill where Genevieve prays. The tradition says Clovis hurled his francisca from where he stood, and the length of the throw fixed the length of the nave: the war-axe of the pagan measuring out the house of God is the whole reign in one gesture. It is built as the dynasty's necropolis. The queen intends to gather her dead here; she does not yet know how many there will be.
suggested_refs: Tour Clovis, Lycée Henri-IV (last vestige of the abbey)
Abbaye Sainte-Geneviève de Paris
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.43, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Paris, the death of Clovis
stops.campa: Clovis dies at Paris in the fifth year after Vouillé, thirty years a king, forty-five years a man, eleven years a Christian. They carry him up Genevieve's hill and lay him in the sanctuary of the church of the Holy Apostles that he and his queen built: the first king of France buried in the first royal church of France. Clotilde walks behind the bier of the husband she gave to God. The kingdom is cut in four for her three sons and Theuderic; the queen, at about thirty-seven, puts on the widowhood she will wear for thirty-four years.
suggested_refs: Tomb of Clovis (recumbent effigy now at Saint-Denis)
Tour Clovis, Lycée Henri-IV
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.43, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

segments.name: La veuve de Saint-Martin: Tours et la vengeance (511-524)

stops.name: Tours, the retreat to the basilica of Saint Martin
stops.campa: The widow leaves the palaces to her sons and comes to Tours, to the tomb of Martin, soldier turned saint, the great intercessor of the Gauls. She takes a house by the basilica and becomes what she was in Geneva before the ring found her: the servant of the poor. Alms with her own hands, vigils in the cold nave, fasting, the long psalms before dawn: Gregory says she made men think of her not as a queen but as God's own handmaid. Rarely, and more rarely with the years, does she go up to Paris. Martin's porch is her court now.
stops.quote: She served there in the church of Saint Martin, with the greatest chastity and kindness, all the days of her life, seldom visiting Paris.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.43
suggested_refs: Basilique Saint-Martin de Tours, the tomb of Saint Martin
Charité de sainte Clotilde imagery (alms to the poor)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.43, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs2.htm

stops.name: Les Andelys, the monastery and the fountain turned to wine
stops.campa: On the Seine's chalk bends in the Vexin the widow founds a monastery for virgins at Andely: the tradition counts it the eldest monastic house of Normandy. In the heat of the building season the workmen groan for drink, and the queen, who has no wine to give them, gives them prayer instead: she kneels at the spring by the works, and the water rises tasting of wine, strength and savor together, until the walls are raised. The fountain keeps her name and her virtue; for fourteen centuries the sick will come to its basin and leave their crutches hanging by the water.
suggested_refs: Fontaine Sainte-Clotilde, Les Andelys
Verrière de sainte Clotilde, collégiale Notre-Dame des Andelys
sources: Vita sanctae Chrothildis (the miracle of the fountain), https://www.ville-andelys.fr/fontaine-sainte-clotilde-2/

stops.name: Paris, the exhortation: avenge my father and my mother
stops.campa: The canon is honest about its saint: the wound at the root never closed. Clotilde calls her sons, Chlodomer, Childebert, Chlothar, and sets before them the sword-death of her father and the river-death of her mother, and asks for Burgundy in payment. The kings take up their mother's feud and march against Sigismund, son of the dead Gundobad. The queen of the alms and the vigils has loosed the Frankish war-machine with her own grief for its banner. Everything that follows, the well, Vézeronce, the murdered grandsons, flows from this hour, and Gregory does not hide it.
stops.quote: Let me not repent, dearest sons, that I have brought you up so tenderly; be indignant, I pray you, at the wrong done to me, and avenge with skill and zeal the death of my father and my mother.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.6
suggested_refs: Lawrence Alma-Tadema, 'The Education of the Children of Clovis' (1861)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.6, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs3.htm

stops.name: The well of Columna (Saint-Sigismond, near Orléans), the feud's bitter fruit
stops.campa: Sigismund of Burgundy, defeated and taken in monk's habit, is carried captive into the Orléanais. There, at the place called Columna, Chlodomer has him thrown down a well with his wife and his sons: the drowned queen of Lyon answered, a generation later, with a drowned king of Burgundy and his drowned children. The vengeance is exact, and it is monstrous, and heaven keeps its own ledger: the well becomes a shrine, Sigismund a martyr-saint whose water cures fevers, and Chlodomer has one year to live. Clotilde's feud is fed, and now it begins to feed on her.
suggested_refs: Puits Saint-Sigismond, church of Saint-Sigismond (Loiret)
Saint Sigismund, king and martyr
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.6, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs3.htm

stops.name: Vézeronce, the death of Chlodomer
stops.campa: On the marshy plain of Vézeronce the Franks meet Godomar's Burgundians. Chlodomer, the son her prayers once lifted from the fever, sees horsemen he takes for his own and spurs into the enemy's midst. They cut him down; his head goes up on a pike above the field, the long royal hair unmistakable against the sky. The Franks, mad with the sight, win the day their king has lost. In the marsh a gilded helmet sinks and waits thirteen centuries for the peat-cutters. At Tours the news comes to Clotilde: the vengeance she asked for has taken her son as its wage.
suggested_refs: The Vézeronce helmet (Musée de l'Ancien Évêché, Grenoble)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.6, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs3.htm

segments.name: Les ciseaux et les épées, la pénitence et le passage (524-545)

stops.name: Paris, the grandmother takes the orphans
stops.campa: Chlodomer leaves three small sons: Theudovald, Gunthar, Chlodovald. Clotilde takes them to herself and raises them in her own house, and Gregory says she loved them with the whole of her surviving heart: the orphan of Lyon gathering orphans, the pattern of her life closing its circle. But the boys are heirs to a third of a kingdom, and their uncles Childebert and Chlothar watch the grandmother's tenderness the way Gundobad once watched a brother's house. Envy, says the canon, begins its work: the love she pours on the children is read in Paris as a crown being prepared.
suggested_refs: The three sons of Chlodomer, Grandes Chroniques imagery
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.18, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs3.htm

stops.name: Paris, the scissors and the swords
stops.campa: The uncles lure the boys from her on the pretext of crowning them, then send Arcadius with scissors and a naked sword: the shears of the cloister, or the blade. Out of the depth of her grief, not weighing her words, the queen answers that she would rather see them dead than shorn, and Arcadius runs with the sentence before she can call it back. Chlothar seizes the elder boy and stabs him; the younger clings to Childebert's knees crying 'Help me, most pious father, lest I die as my brother died,' and Childebert, weeping, gives him up. Ten years old, and seven. Her own tongue sprang the trap.
stops.quote: It is better for me to see them dead than shorn, if they are not to be raised to the kingship.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.18
suggested_refs: The scissors and the sword before Clotilde, Grandes Chroniques de France
19th-c. history painting of the sons of Chlodomer
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.18, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs3.htm

stops.name: Paris, the funeral of the little kings
stops.campa: The grandmother comes for the bodies. She lays the two boys on one bier and follows them up Genevieve's hill with a great singing of psalms, her grief past all consoling, to the church of the Holy Apostles: the necropolis she built for kings receiving its smallest kings. She buries them beside Clovis: the grandfather who conquered Gaul and the grandsons murdered for a third of it, under one roof, by her doing and her undoing both. From this day the canon shows her wholly God's: there is nothing left in Paris for her but graves.
stops.quote: She placed their bodies on a bier and followed them, with great singing of psalms and in boundless grief, to the church of Saint Peter, and buried them side by side.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.18
suggested_refs: Abbaye Sainte-Geneviève (church of the Holy Apostles), Paris
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.18, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs3.htm

stops.name: Nogent on the Seine (Saint-Cloud), the escape of Clodoald
stops.campa: The third boy, Chlodovald, is snatched from the slaughter by brave men and hidden past all his uncles' searching. Grown, he does with his own hand what the scissors threatened: he cuts the royal hair himself, and with it cuts away kingdom, feud and blade forever. Clerk, then priest, he settles at Nogent on the Seine below Paris, builds his hermitage, gives his goods to the poor, and dies in the odor of sanctity. The village takes his name and keeps it: Saint-Cloud. Of all Clotilde's line of grief he is the one who ends it: the Merovingian who refused.
stops.quote: He cut his hair with his own hand and became a clerk, and giving himself to good works he was ordained priest, and died a priest.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.18
suggested_refs: Église Saint-Clodoald, Saint-Cloud
Reliquary of Saint Clodoald
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.18, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs3.htm

stops.name: Tours, the storm that stopped a war
stops.campa: Her surviving sons turn on each other at last: Childebert and his nephew Theudebert march against Chlothar, who shelters in a forest camp behind felled trees. Clotilde hears of it at Tours, goes to the tomb of Martin, and stays in prayer through the whole night, asking that the war of her sons not come to battle. At dawn the sky answers: lightning, hail and screaming wind fall on the aggressors' army, tents flattened, horses scattered, men flogged to the ground, while on Chlothar's camp not one drop falls. The kings send messengers, and there is peace. Gregory writes the attribution himself.
stops.quote: Let no one doubt that this was a miracle of the blessed Martin, granted by the prayers of the queen.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.28
suggested_refs: Tomb of Saint Martin, Tours
The night vigil of Clotilde (hagiographic imagery)
sources: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum III.28, https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/historiens/gregoire/francs3.htm

stops.name: Tours, the death of the queen, full of days
stops.campa: On the third of June, in the episcopate of Injuriosus, Queen Clotilde dies at Tours beside the saint she served for thirty-four years. She is about seventy. She has outlived her father's murder, her mother's river, her husband, her firstborn in his chrisom-robes, her son on the pike at Vézeronce, and the two grandsons her own words could not save; she has converted a king, a dynasty, and through them a nation. Gregory closes the account like a psalm: full of days and rich in good works, she goes to the God she never once stopped talking to.
stops.quote: Queen Clotilde, full of days and rich in good works, died at the city of Tours in the time of bishop Injuriosus.

stops.name: Paris, carried home: the burial beside Clovis and Genevieve
stops.campa: With a great singing of psalms they carry the queen from Tours to Paris, her sons Childebert and Chlothar, the killers of her grandsons, the last of her children, walking as her heirs. On Genevieve's hill they lay her in the sanctuary of the Holy Apostles, at the side of King Clovis, near Genevieve, near the two little kings on their single bier: all her dead gathered under the roof she raised. The church will take Genevieve's name; the queen will take the altars of France: SAINTE CLOTILDE. Her Reims font faces Joan's coronation across nine centuries, and her line of grief closes at last, feud and forgiveness bound into the same stone.
stops.quote: With a great singing of psalms she was carried to Paris, and buried by her sons in the sanctuary of the basilica of Saint Peter, at the side of King Clovis.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum IV.1
